title: Searching for Population III stars with line intensity mapping cross-correlations
comment: 21+10 pages, 12+3 figures; submitted to PRD
summary: Decades of searches for Population III stars in individual galaxies have yielded a few potential candidates, but a statistically robust characterization of the demographics of the first stars in the lowest-mass systems remains elusive. Line intensity mapping (LIM), an observational technique that measures fluctuations in the aggregate emission from the entire galaxy population --- including the faintest sources --- offers an alternative strategy that is especially well-suited for the Pop III era. With the recent launch of SPHEREx and the rapid development of a number of complementary LIM studies, we are poised to place some of the first LIM constraints on sites of star formation at high-redshift. In this work, we expand an analytical model for LIM power spectra, Zeus21/oLIMpus, to include Pop III stars and the emission lines identified as diagnostic signatures of star formation with a low-metallicity, top-heavy IMF, such as H$α$ and HeII. We introduce a flexible framework to estimate the measurement uncertainties associated with instrument and survey configurations, and apply these to study LIM signatures of the first stars in mock surveys carried out with SPHEREx and potential next-generation instruments. We quantify the sensitivity of the LIM signal to variations in Pop II and III parameters and forecast joint limits that can be placed on the Pop III star formation efficiency (SFE) and IMF shape with SPHEREx. We find that next-generation instruments will be necessary to comprehensively survey the Pop III theoretical landscape --- both with respect to `classical' and `exotic' Pop III models --- and identify design improvements that will enable such studies. Finally, we carry out a Fisher analysis to characterize synergies between SPHEREx and JWST, suggesting that joint constraints on the Pop III SFE and extensions to conventional Pop III models may be within reach.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Zeus21/oLIMpus analytical model for line intensity mapping to include Population III stars, enabling predictions for Hα and HeII emission signatures in low-metallicity, top-heavy IMF star formation. The authors develop a flexible uncertainty framework for instrument configuration and apply it to forecast SPHEREx and next-generation LIM surveys, finding that next-gen instruments are needed for comprehensive Pop III surveys and that joint SPHEREx+JWST constraints on Pop III star formation efficiency and IMF shape are feasible.
AI.motivation: Population III stars, the first stars in the universe, have only a few tentative individual detections and no statistically robust characterization of their demographics in low-mass galaxies. Line intensity mapping offers a complementary approach uniquely suited for probing the Pop III era, and with SPHEREx recently launched alongside growing LIM efforts, there is an opportunity to place the first LIM constraints on high-redshift star formation sites.
AI.method: The authors extend the analytical LIM power spectrum model Zeus21/oLIMpus to incorporate Pop III stars and diagnostic emission lines (Hα, HeII) characteristic of low-metallicity top-heavy IMF star formation. They introduce a flexible framework for estimating measurement uncertainties from instrument and survey configurations, then apply this to mock surveys with SPHEREx and potential next-generation instruments. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the dependence of LIM signals on Pop II/III parameters, including Fisher analysis for SPHEREx-JWST synergies.
AI.result: Next-generation instruments (beyond SPHEREx) will be necessary to comprehensively survey the full Pop III theoretical landscape, covering both classical and exotic Pop III models. The authors identify specific design improvements that enable such studies. Fisher analysis suggests that joint SPHEREx+JWST constraints on Pop III star formation efficiency, IMF shape, and extensions to conventional Pop III models may be achievable.
AI.conclusion: The expanded Zeus21/oLIMpus framework demonstrates that line intensity mapping can constrain Population III star formation, though SPHEREx alone may not fully cover the Pop III parameter space. Joint observations combining SPHEREx and JWST offer promising synergies for constraining the Pop III SFE and IMF, bringing the first statistical characterization of the first stars within reach as next-generation LIM instruments are developed.

title: Misaligned or chaotic? A strong break of axial symmetry in the local LRD J1025 revealed with VLT/FORS2 spectropolarimetry
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact active galactic nuclei (AGN) with unusual spectral energy distributions and broad Balmer emission, candidate signposts of rapid black-hole growth. We present VLT/FORS2 optical linear spectropolarimetry of the closest known LRD, SDSS J102530.29+140207.3, at z=0.1. In total light, we detect spatially extended narrow-H$α$ emission, probably tracing the host galaxy. We measure a nearly grey continuum polarisation $p_{\rm cont}=1.53\pm0.04$(rand.)$\pm$0.20(syst.) per cent, while broad H$α$ is less polarised, $p_{\rm Hα}=0.58-0.84$ per cent. We rule out polarisation by Milky Way dust and dilution by an unpolarised line. The polarised continuum with a depolarised line resembles local Seyfert-1 nuclei and favours a single dominant source over multi-source explanations. After Stokes-continuum subtraction, broad H$α$ shows no blue-to-red swing, but there is a significant (48$\pm$4)$^\circ$ continuum-to-line offset in polarisation angle. This implies a break of axial symmetry inside this object, posing interesting geometrical challenges to all existing LRD models and frameworks. We discuss different possible origins of this symmetry break and possible paths to discriminate between them with future observations.

AI.tldr: Spectropolarimetry of the closest Little Red Dot (LRD), SDSS J102530.29+140207.3 at z=0.1, reveals a grey continuum polarization of 1.53% with a less-polarized broad Hα line, and a significant 48° polarization-angle offset between continuum and line, indicating broken axial symmetry that challenges existing LRD models.
AI.motivation: LRDs are compact AGN with unusual properties that may mark rapid black-hole growth, but their nature remains unclear. Spectropolarimetry of the closest LRD offers a unique opportunity to constrain the dominant emission source and test existing LRD models.
AI.method: VLT/FORS2 optical linear spectropolarimetry of the nearest LRD at z=0.1. Analysis includes separating continuum and broad-Hα polarization, Stokes-continuum subtraction to search for velocity-dependent polarization swings, and comparison with Milky Way dust polarization and Seyfert-1 templates.
AI.result: Measure near-grey continuum polarization of 1.53% and weaker broad Hα polarization (0.58–0.84%). A 48±4° continuum-to-line polarization-angle offset is found with no blue-to-red swing, implying a break of axial symmetry inside the object. Milky Way dust and unpolarized-line dilution are excluded.
AI.conclusion: The polarized-continuum/depolarized-line behavior resembles Seyfert-1 nuclei, favoring a single dominant AGN source. However, the significant polarization-angle offset between continuum and line poses geometrical challenges to all existing LRD models, requiring future observations to discriminate between possible symmetry-breaking origins.

title: Quiescent Host Galaxies of Extended Quasars Revealed by Spectrophotometric Decomposition
comment: Published in The Astrophysical Journal, 1004, 13 (2026), 20 pages, 20 figures
summary: Previous works of low-redshift quasar host galaxies have focused on compact quasars and found that their host galaxies are mainly star-forming galaxies. Here we present a study of host galaxies for quasars with extended morphologies in ground-based optical images. We select a sample of more than 1000 type 1 quasars at redshift $0.1<z<1$ that are classified as extended objects by DESI. Combining high-resolution spectra from DESI and high-quality images from Subaru HSC, we develop a spectrophotometric decomposition technique to iteratively decompose each quasar into an AGN component and its host galaxy. The technique can effectively break the degeneracy between the AGN and host components and capture the host spectral features. Our results show that the host galaxies of most quasars have low star-formation rates (SFRs) and low specific SFRs, indicating that they are quiescent galaxies. Many of them exhibit prominent post-starburst features with the existence of significant old stellar populations. These properties are quite different from the nature of compact quasars with star-forming host galaxies. In addition, the relation between the black hole mass and stellar mass for our sample is broadly consistent with the canonical local relations. This work is complementary to the previous studies and suggests that the host galaxies of low-redshift quasars are more diverse than what was thought.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes host galaxies of low-redshift quasars with extended morphologies using DESI spectra and Subaru HSC images. Unlike previous work on compact quasars (which host star-forming galaxies), most extended quasars have quiescent host galaxies with low SFRs, many showing post-starburst features. The black hole-stellar mass relation is consistent with local relations, revealing that quasar host galaxies are more diverse than previously thought.
AI.motivation: Previous studies of low-redshift quasar host galaxies focused on compact quasars, finding predominantly star-forming hosts. This work aims to extend the picture by studying quasars with extended morphologies, which had been largely unexplored, to determine whether the nature of quasar host galaxies is truly homogeneous or more diverse.
AI.method: The authors select over 1000 type 1 quasars at 0.1<z<1 classified as extended objects by DESI. They combine high-resolution DESI spectra with high-quality Subaru HSC imaging and develop an iterative spectrophotometric decomposition technique to separate each quasar into an AGN component and a host galaxy component, effectively breaking the degeneracy between the two.
AI.result: Most host galaxies of the extended quasars exhibit low SFRs and low specific SFRs, indicating quiescent galaxies. Many show prominent post-starburst features alongside significant old stellar populations, contrasting sharply with the star-forming hosts of compact quasars. The black hole mass--stellar mass relation is broadly consistent with canonical local relations.
AI.conclusion: The host galaxies of low-redshift quasars are more diverse than previously assumed: while compact quasars reside in star-forming hosts, extended quasars primarily reside in quiescent/post-starburst hosts. This work complements prior studies and highlights the need to consider morphological diversity when characterizing quasar host galaxy evolution.

title: Changing-Look AGNs from DESI. VI. Host Galaxies
comment: Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal; 20 pages, 12 figures
summary: Changing-look (CL) AGNs trace rapid changes in nuclear activity, but their connection to host galaxy properties remains unclear. We present a study of the host galaxies of 105 CL AGNs previously selected by comparing DESI and SDSS data. We apply a two-epoch spectrophotometric decomposition to the DESI and SDSS spectra of the 105 objects. Meanwhile, HSC images are used to constrain their varying AGN components and non-varying stellar population components. We find that 79 of the 105 (75.2%) CL AGN hosts are quiescent galaxies, and 31/105 (29.5%) also show post-starburst signatures. We focus on 82 CL AGNs with extended host emission in the HSC images and compare them with extended quasars at similar redshift and stellar mass. Their star formation activity, Balmer absorption, and quiescent fractions are broadly consistent with those of the comparison quasars, although post-starburst hosts are more common among the CL AGNs. Our CL AGNs with extended host emission are more often quiescent than those with compact morphology, but this difference is not apparent after matching in redshift and stellar mass. The $\mathrm{O\, \small II}$ and $\mathrm{O\, \small III}$ narrow lines show no population-wide response to the continuum and broad line changes, consistent with the slower response expected from the narrow line region. Together, these results favor changes in the central supermassive black hole accretion rate as the main origin of the CL transitions.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the host galaxies of 105 changing-look AGNs (selected from DESI/SDSS comparison) via two-epoch spectrophotometric decomposition and HSC imaging. 75.2% of hosts are quiescent, 29.5% show post-starburst signatures, and their properties are broadly consistent with comparison quasars. Narrow-line emission shows no population-wide response to continuum changes, favoring central accretion-rate changes as the main origin of CL transitions.
AI.motivation: Changing-look AGNs offer unique insight into rapid nuclear activity variations, but their connection to host galaxy properties (e.g., star formation, stellar populations) remains poorly understood. This study aims to clarify whether CL transitions are driven by changes in the black hole accretion rate or by host-galaxy-level processes.
AI.method: The authors apply a two-epoch spectrophotometric decomposition to DESI and SDSS spectra of 105 CL AGNs to separate varying AGN components from non-varying stellar populations. HSC imaging is used to constrain the spatial extent of AGN and stellar components. Host properties are compared to matching extended quasars in redshift and stellar mass.
AI.result: 79/105 (75.2%) CL AGN hosts are quiescent, and 31/105 (29.5%) show post-starburst signatures. For the 82 CL AGNs with extended host emission, star formation activity, Balmer absorption, and quiescent fractions are broadly consistent with comparison quasars, though post-starburst hosts are more common among CL AGNs. Narrow O II and O III lines show no population-wide response to continuum/broad-line changes.
AI.conclusion: The results support changes in the central supermassive black hole accretion rate as the primary driver of CL transitions, rather than host-galaxy-scale processes. The lack of narrow-line response is consistent with the expected longer time delay of the narrow line region.

title: Peering through the dip: IXPE unveils the extended scattering environment of GX 13+1
comment: Submitted on A&A
summary: Neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries feature complex accretion geometries, often including an accretion disk corona or disk winds. Here, a study of the highly inclined dipping source GX 13+1, using coordinated observations from the IXPE, NuSTAR, and Swift-XRT, is presented; this is the first time that such a campaign was conducted to monitor its periodic dip. Our analysis reveals significant variations in polarimetric properties tracking the dip. At the center of the dip, the polarization degree reaches a maximum of ${\sim}$9% (at more than $8σ$ confidence level). This is accompanied by a highly significant polarization angle rotation of roughly 60$^\circ$ when passing from the dip to the subsequent off-dip state. Furthermore, the dip state exhibits energy-dependent polarization. By modeling the polarization during the periodic dip, we constrain the geometry of the scattering medium. In the scenario of an oblate extended accretion disk corona (ADC), an equatorial radius at least 1.5 times its polar radius is needed with $τ{\sim}0.3$. Alternatively, the results can be modeled as scattering in a disk wind with a most probable electron density of $1.3\times10^{14}$ cm$^{-3}$ and an opening angle near 40$^\circ$, corresponding to an optical depth of ${\sim}0.2$. The obtained results highlight the crucial role of X-ray polarimetric data to unveil the geometry of the extended scattering environment surrounding the accretion disks, advancing our understanding of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries.

AI.tldr: This study uses coordinated IXPE, NuSTAR, and Swift-XRT observations of the dipping neutron star LMXB GX 13+1 to track its periodic dip. Polarization degree peaks at ~9% (8σ) at dip center with a ~60° polarization angle rotation, revealing the geometry of the extended scattering medium—either an oblate ADC (equatorial radius ≥1.5× polar radius, τ~0.3) or a disk wind (electron density 1.3×10^14 cm^-3, opening angle ~40°, τ~0.2).
AI.motivation: To constrain the complex accretion geometry—including accretion disk corona and disk winds—of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries using X-ray polarimetry, taking advantage of the periodic dipping behavior in GX 13+1 to probe the scattering environment.
AI.method: Coordinated multi-observatory campaign with IXPE (polarimetry), NuSTAR, and Swift-XRT (spectral/timing) to monitor the periodic dip of GX 13+1. Polarimetric properties were analyzed as a function of dip phase, including energy-dependent polarization, and modeled with accretion disk corona and disk wind scattering geometries.
AI.result: Significant polarimetric variations track the dip: polarization degree reaches ~9% (>8σ) at dip center, accompanied by a ~60° polarization angle rotation between dip and off-dip states. The dip shows energy-dependent polarization. Modeling constrains either an oblate ADC with equatorial radius ≥1.5× polar radius and τ~0.3, or a disk wind with electron density 1.3×10^14 cm^-3, opening angle ~40°, and optical depth ~0.2.
AI.conclusion: X-ray polarimetric data play a crucial role in unveiling the geometry of the extended scattering environment surrounding accretion disks, significantly advancing the understanding of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries.

title: Fishing for Jellyfish Galaxies: Exploring ram-pressure stripping with crowd science
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables
summary: Aims: We present the first results of Fishing for Jellyfish Galaxies, a pilot citizen-science project using Zooniverse to identify galaxies undergoing ram-pressure stripping (RPS). Methods: Volunteers visually inspected colour images of late-type galaxies from the Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey, from a sample of 49,703 galaxies selected within $4 \times R_{500}$ of clusters and groups, restricted to galaxies brighter than 19th magnitude in the g and r bands, and with a minimum half-light radius of 2 arcseconds, to aid classification. We detail our data processing, including debiasing classifications and optimising vote-fraction thresholds to maximise completeness and purity, calibrated against a ground-truth set of pre-labelled galaxies. Results: Our final catalogue contains 6739 jellyfish candidates (6621 new), 5430 merger candidates, and 29,729 undisturbed galaxies, with 3910 jellyfish exhibiting prominent tail-like morphologies. We find that the fraction of RPS candidates rises from ~10% in galaxy groups to ~20-30% in massive clusters, confirming the findings of previous studies carried out on smaller samples. For the subset of our RPS candidate sample with spectroscopic data, we measure a median clustercentric velocity 53% higher than the general cluster population, consistent with galaxies in early stages of accretion into the cluster. They are also typically late-type blue galaxies with elevated star-formation rates, in agreement with expectations. These results demonstrate that citizen scientists can reliably identify galaxies that undergo environmental processes. We provide the initial release of 37,599 visually classified galaxies as a resource for future studies of galaxy transformation in clusters.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first results of Fishing for Jellyfish Galaxies, a citizen-science project using Zooniverse to identify galaxies undergoing ram-pressure stripping (RPS). Volunteers classified 49,703 late-type galaxies from DESI Legacy Survey data, producing a catalogue of 6,739 jellyfish candidates, 5,430 mergers, and 29,729 undisturbed galaxies. The fraction of RPS candidates rises from ~10% in groups to ~20-30% in massive clusters, and RPS candidates show elevated clustercentric velocities and star-formation rates, confirming expectations of environmental transformation in clusters.
AI.motivation: To identify galaxies undergoing ram-pressure stripping (jellyfish galaxies) at a scale larger than previous studies, using citizen science to overcome the limitations of automatic detection methods and provide a large, high-quality catalogue for studying environmental processes in clusters.
AI.method: Volunteers visually inspected colour images of late-type galaxies from the Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey, selected within 4×R500 of clusters and groups (49,703 galaxies brighter than 19th mag in g and r bands with minimum half-light radius of 2 arcseconds). Classifications were debiased and vote-fraction thresholds optimised against a ground-truth set of pre-labelled galaxies to maximise completeness and purity.
AI.result: Final catalogue contains 6,739 jellyfish candidates (6,621 new), 5,430 merger candidates, and 29,729 undisturbed galaxies, with 3,910 jellyfish exhibiting prominent tail-like morphologies. RPS fraction rises from ~10% in groups to ~20-30% in massive clusters. RPS candidates show median clustercentric velocity 53% higher than the general cluster population and are typically late-type blue galaxies with elevated star-formation rates.
AI.conclusion: Citizen scientists can reliably identify galaxies undergoing environmental processes. The results confirm previous findings on smaller samples and the initial release of 37,599 visually classified galaxies provides a valuable resource for future studies of galaxy transformation in clusters.

title: Deep Learning-Based Classification and Analysis of Pulsar Candidates in Fermi-LAT Unassociated Sources
comment: Accepted in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: The Large Area Telescope (LAT) has revolutionized our understanding of the high-energy sky, yet approximately one-third of the sources in the Fourth Fermi-LAT Source Catalog (4FGL) remain unassociated. Conventional machine learning, such as Decision Trees, often treat spectral features as independent tabular entries, neglecting the sequential topological information inherent in the Spectral Energy Distribution (SED). We aim to classify unassociated Fermi-LAT sources by exploiting the intrinsic shape of their spectra and variability features, avoiding the use of galactic coordinates as training features. Our primary objective is to generate a high-confidence list of PSRs candidates, further distinguishing between Young Pulsars (YPs) and Millisecond Pulsars (MSPs). We developed a hierarchical deep learning framework based on a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN), named TabularResCNN. This architecture treats the spectral data from the 4FGL catalog, allowing the model spectral shape. The classification is performed in two stages: first discriminating between AGNs and PSRs, and subsequently categorizing PSRs into YPs and MSPs. We implemented a cost-sensitive learning strategy to handle class imbalance and utilized Grad-CAM techniques to ensure the physical interpretability of the model's decisions. Applying this framework to 2563 unassociated sources, we identified 1136 AGNs and 202 high-confidence PSR candidates (166 YPs, 36 MSPs), increasing the pulsar population by more than 60%. They exhibit strong astrophysical consistency: YPs are confined to the Galactic plane, MSPs show a broader vertical distribution, and AGNs are isotropic. Furthermore, we identified 5 out of 5 PSRs recently confirmed by FAST. The proposed 1D-CNN framework isolates PSRs candidates based on intrinsic spectral and temporal properties, minimizing spatial bias.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TabularResCNN, a hierarchical 1D-CNN framework that classifies unassociated Fermi-LAT 4FGL sources by exploiting intrinsic spectral shape (SED) and variability features without using galactic coordinates. It identifies 202 high-confidence pulsar candidates (166 YPs, 36 MSPs) from 2563 unassociated sources, increasing the known pulsar population by over 60%, and demonstrates strong astrophysical consistency.
AI.motivation: Approximately one-third of sources in the 4FGL catalog remain unassociated. Conventional machine learning methods, such as Decision Trees, treat spectral features as independent tabular entries, neglecting the sequential topological information inherent in the Spectral Energy Distribution (SED).
AI.method: A hierarchical deep learning framework based on a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) called TabularResCNN. It treats spectral data from the 4FGL catalog to leverage spectral shape. Classification is done in two stages: (1) AGNs vs. PSRs, then (2) PSRs categorized into YPs and MSPs. Cost-sensitive learning handles class imbalance, and Grad-CAM techniques ensure physical interpretability. Galactic coordinates are excluded from training features to minimize spatial bias.
AI.result: Applied to 2563 unassociated sources, the framework identified 1136 AGNs and 202 high-confidence PSR candidates (166 YPs, 36 MSPs), increasing the pulsar population by over 60%. The candidates exhibit strong astrophysical consistency: YPs confined to the Galactic plane, MSPs with broader vertical distribution, and AGNs isotropic. Additionally, 5 of 5 PSRs recently confirmed by FAST were correctly identified.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 1D-CNN framework isolates pulsar candidates based on intrinsic spectral and temporal properties, minimizing spatial bias and yielding physically consistent, high-confidence classifications of unassociated Fermi-LAT sources.

title: SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM): The Integrated Light and Internal Rotation of Omega Centauri
comment: 16 pages, 13 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM) is a wide-field integral field spectroscopic survey of the Southern Milky Way plane, the Magellanic Clouds, and nearby Local Group galaxies. We use Early Science observations of the whole body of the nearest nuclear cluster, Omega Centauri, to extend the LVM beyond its primary interstellar-medium science case. The wide LVM field allows us to precisely map $ω$ Cen's line-of-sight rotation out to $\sim 3r_{HL}$ or $15^\prime$, reaching a maximum value of $(8.4 \pm 0.8)$ km s$^{-1}$ at $r \approx 4.7^\prime$. Within the central region, comparisons with existing VLT MUSE oMEGACat data show explicitly that the unresolved-light signal is dominated by a small number of bright stars, with an effective sample size of only $\sim$12 per resolution element. Using Gaia DR3 as an external reference, we verify that the SDSS-V's LVM reduction pipeline recovers integrated stellar fluxes to 1-4 % across six magnitudes of surface brightness. Our resulting total spectrum of $ω$ Cen is one of the highest S/N integrated spectrum for any globular or nuclear star cluster. We use it to test four widely-used SSP template libraries against resolved age-metallicity ground truth from oMEGACat. All templates recover an old, metal-poor population. But, even at S/N $\sim$1300, the inferred mean ages and mean [Fe/H] vary by $\sim$7 Gyr and $\sim$0.4 dex, respectively, across libraries and wavelength ranges, reflecting a systematic floor for integrated-light studies of old multi-population systems.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM) survey beyond its primary interstellar-medium science case by using Early Science observations to map Omega Centauri, the nearest nuclear cluster. The authors measure its line-of-sight rotation out to ~3r_HL, verify flux recovery accuracy against Gaia DR3, and use a high S/N integrated spectrum to test four SSP template libraries against resolved age-metallicity ground truth, finding systematic variations of ~7 Gyr and ~0.4 dex in inferred ages and metallicities across libraries.
AI.motivation: To push the LVM survey beyond its original interstellar-medium focus by demonstrating its utility for studying globular/nuclear star clusters, and to quantify the systematic limitations of integrated-light stellar population studies of old, multi-population systems.
AI.method: Early Science observations of Omega Centauri with the wide-field LVM integral field spectrograph; comparison with VLT MUSE oMEGACat data to assess unresolved-light star-dominance; calibration against Gaia DR3 to verify flux recovery across six magnitudes of surface brightness; testing four SSP template libraries against resolved oMEGACat age-metallicity ground truth using the high S/N integrated spectrum.
AI.result: Measured rotation of Omega Centauri reaching (8.4 ± 0.8) km/s at r ≈ 4.7 arcmin; found unresolved-light signal dominated by ~12 bright stars per resolution element; verified LVM pipeline recovers integrated stellar fluxes to 1-4% accuracy; produced one of the highest S/N integrated spectra for a globular/nuclear cluster; found all SSP templates recover an old metal-poor population, but inferred mean ages and [Fe/H] vary by ~7 Gyr and ~0.4 dex across libraries even at S/N ~1300.
AI.conclusion: LVM can be successfully extended to stellar-population science cases beyond interstellar-medium studies. However, integrated-light studies of old multi-population systems suffer a systematic floor of ~7 Gyr in age and ~0.4 dex in metallicity due to template library and wavelength range choices, regardless of high S/N.

title: Energy-dependent Optical/Near-infrared and X-ray Correlations in Swift J1727.8-1613
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present a timing analysis of the black hole transient Swift J1727.8-1613 during its intermediate state. We use coordinated broadband X-ray observations from Insight-HXMT (2-150 keV), together with optical data from ULTRACAM (g_s and i_s bands) and near-infrared data from HAWK-I (K_s band), obtained on 2023 September 9. As shown by previous studies, the Fourier power spectrum shows a strong quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) in the K_s, i_s and X-ray bands. Cross-correlation analysis reveals a complex coupling between the optical/near-infrared (OIR) and X-ray emission, including a delayed optical anti-correlation, a strong infrared correlation, and a pronounced dependence of these features on X-ray energy, suggesting multiple Comptonisation regions. In contrast, the lag properties do not change at the QPO frequency, displaying an OIR lag of ~60-80 ms up to 150 keV. We discuss these results in the context of small-scale jet and hot accretion flow scenarios.

AI.tldr: Timing analysis of the black hole transient Swift J1727.8-1613 during its intermediate state using coordinated Insight-HXMT (2-150 keV), ULTRACAM (g_s, i_s), and HAWK-I (K_s) observations from 2023 September 9. Cross-correlation reveals complex OIR/X-ray coupling including delayed optical anti-correlation and strong IR correlation dependent on X-ray energy, with a constant ~60-80 ms OIR lag at the QPO frequency up to 150 keV, discussed in the context of small-scale jet and hot accretion flow scenarios.
AI.motivation: To characterize the multi-wavelength timing properties and coupling between optical/near-infrared and X-ray emission in the intermediate state of a black hole transient, to distinguish between small-scale jet and hot accretion flow emission mechanisms.
AI.method: Fourier power spectral analysis to identify QPOs across K_s, i_s, and X-ray bands; cross-correlation analysis between OIR and X-ray light curves to examine lags and energy-dependent coupling; comparison of lag properties across optical, NIR, and X-ray energy bands.
AI.result: A strong QPO is present in K_s, i_s, and X-ray bands. Cross-correlation shows a delayed optical anti-correlation, a strong infrared correlation, and an energy-dependent behavior of these features suggesting multiple Comptonisation regions. The OIR lag (~60-80 ms) does not vary with frequency and persists up to 150 keV.
AI.conclusion: The constant lag up to high X-ray energies and the energy-dependent coupling complexity favor scenarios involving multiple Comptonisation regions; results are discussed in light of small-scale jet and hot accretion flow models to explain the OIR-X-ray emission geometry.

title: EWOCS-VIII: Internal kinematics and expansion of Westerlund 1 from VVVX proper motions
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Westerlund 1 (Wd1) is the most massive young star cluster known in the Milky Way and a key laboratory for studying the early dynamical evolution of massive clusters. Owing to its high extinction, the internal kinematics of its intermediate-mass stellar population remain largely unexplored. We aim to characterize the internal kinematic properties of Wd1 using a homogeneous census of near-infrared (NIR) selected cluster members and their proper motions (PMs). We considered PMs from the VIRAC2 catalog, based on multi-epoch VVV/VVVX observations. For $1286$ candidate members previously identified through NIR photometry and astrometry (Paper I), we computed their PMs relative to the cluster mean motion and analyzed them as a function of position and radius. We also investigate radial trends, test the robustness of the results against the assumed cluster center, and search for preferred directions of motion. We detect a statistically significant signature of expansion in the outer regions of Wd1, with the radial component of the relative PMs increasing with distance from the cluster center. The expansion appears asymmetric, with the strongest gradient detected along a PA$=84\degree \pm 8\degree$ in the plane of the sky and with $5.9σ$ significance. We also find hints for inward radial motions in the central region, consistent with ongoing mass segregation, but only at $\approx 2σ$ significance. Taken together, these results are consistent with a nearly monolithic formation scenario.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the internal kinematics of the massive young star cluster Westerlund 1 using NIR-selected cluster members and proper motions from the VIRAC2 catalog based on VVV/VVVX data. The authors detect a significant asymmetric expansion in the outer regions of the cluster (5.9σ significance along PA=84°±8°) and find weak hints of inward radial motions in the central region (~2σ), consistent with a nearly monolithic formation scenario.
AI.motivation: Westerlund 1 is the most massive young star cluster in the Milky Way and a key laboratory for studying early dynamical evolution of massive clusters. However, due to high extinction, the internal kinematics of its intermediate-mass stellar population remain largely unexplored, motivating this kinematic study.
AI.method: The authors used proper motions from the VIRAC2 catalog (based on multi-epoch VVV/VVVX observations) for 1286 candidate cluster members previously identified via NIR photometry and astrometry. They computed proper motions relative to the cluster mean motion, analyzed them as a function of position and radius, investigated radial trends, tested robustness against assumed cluster center, and searched for preferred motion directions.
AI.result: A statistically significant asymmetric expansion signature is detected in the outer regions of Wd1, with the radial component of relative proper motions increasing with distance from the cluster center. The strongest gradient is along PA=84°±8° with 5.9σ significance. Hints of inward radial motions in the central region are found at ~2σ, consistent with ongoing mass segregation.
AI.conclusion: The combination of outer expansion and central inward motions is consistent with a nearly monolithic formation scenario for Westerlund 1.

title: Strongly Magnetized Super-Eddington Accretion: How Spin and Accretion Rate Regulate Energy Output and Mass Loss
comment: 15 main figures, 4 tables, submitted
summary: Strongly magnetized super-Eddington accretion flows power many important astrophysical systems, but how black hole parameters control their output is unclear. We present 32 general relativistic radiation magnetohydrodynamics simulations of super-Eddington magnetically arrested disks onto stellar-mass black holes, varying mass ($M_{\rm BH}= 5, 15, 30\,M_{\odot}$), spin ($a=0,0.9$), and accretion rate ($\dot{M}_{\rm acc} \approx 1-2000\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$). We find that black hole spin and accretion rate jointly regulate wind loss rates and energy output efficiencies, while black hole mass has no effect over the mass range studied here. The BH accretes only $10-40\%$ of the mass supplied to the accretion flow, while the rest is expelled in winds. This accretion fraction decreases with mass supply rate and is lower for high-spin systems. Both spin states produce strong magnetically driven outflows. For $a = 0$, the wind kinetic, radiative, and electromagnetic efficiencies are modest and show little variation across the full simulated range of accretion rates. For $a = 0.9$, both wind power and jet power increase super-linearly with $\dot{M}_{\rm acc}$, with the jet power saturating beyond $\dot{M}_{\rm acc} \sim 100\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$. Radiation is strongly beamed along the funnel, with inverse beaming factors exceeding $100$ for high-spin, high-$\dot{m}$ models viewed face-on. Our results establish that rapid BH spin boosts energy-extraction efficiency, while high accretion rate amplifies total power. We provide scaling relations for luminosities, jet power, accretion ratio, and beaming, offering a framework for interpreting observations of ULXs and other super-Eddington systems.

title: Determining Total Infrared Luminosities from Submm Measurements of High Redshift Galaxies
comment: accepted by ApJ
summary: Determining total infrared luminosities for very high redshift galaxies is important to estimate the rate of star formation in heavily dust-embedded environments. It is also challenging because the most sensitive far infrared observatory, Herschel, was limited in sensitivity and its deepest measurements are subject to confusion noise. Thus, these determinations largely depend on ALMA, observing in the mm- and/or submm-wavelengths, which sample only the long-wavelength part of the spectral energy distributions (SEDs). Luminosities are conventionally estimated with modified blackbody fits to these measurements, but do not include the emission in the mid-infrared by warmer dust; there is evidence that this mid-IR component may be relatively strong in very high-redshift galaxies compared with local ones. A correction factor must be applied to the modified black body luminosities to derive the total infrared luminosity. We study infrared SEDs using simulations tuned to galactic conditions typical of high-z galaxies. We find that the different behaviors of infrared SEDs are dominated by a single key physical parameter, the luminosity density. This allows us to estimate the corrections for the missing mid-infrared luminosity in a general way. We find that a factor of ~ 1.6 - 1.7 (0.2 dex) is appropriate in most circumstances, with a larger factor of ~ 1.75 - 1.85 (~ 0.25 dex) up to 2 (0.3 dex) necessary for high redshift (z > 4) galaxies at the highest luminosities, > 10^{12} Lsun. These corrections are needed to estimate star formation rates based on total infrared luminosity.

It finds that luminosity density is the key parameter governing SED behavior, enabling a general correction factor (~1.6-1.7, or 0.2 dex) for missing mid-IR emission when using modified blackbody fits from ALMA observations. Larger corrections (~1.75-1.85, up to 2) are required for the most luminous (L > 10^12 Lsun) galaxies at z > 4.
AI.motivation: Determining total IR luminosities of high-redshift galaxies is critical for estimating star formation rates in dusty galaxies, but Herschel's sensitivity limits and ALMA's sampling of only the long-wavelength SED portion mean that mid-IR warm dust emission is systematically missing from modified blackbody fits. Evidence suggests this mid-IR component is relatively stronger at high redshift, so correction factors are needed.
AI.method: The authors use simulations tuned to galactic conditions typical of high-z galaxies to study infrared SED behavior. They identify luminosity density as the dominant physical parameter controlling SED differences and derive general correction factors for the missing mid-infrared luminosity based on this parameter.
AI.result: A factor of ~1.6-1.7 (0.2 dex) is appropriate for most circumstances. For the most luminous galaxies (> 10^12 Lsun) at z > 4, a larger correction of ~1.75-1.85 (~0.25 dex), up to 2 (0.3 dex), is necessary.
AI.conclusion: These correction factors are essential for accurately converting modified blackbody luminosities derived from ALMA mm/submm observations into total infrared luminosities, which in turn are needed to estimate star formation rates in heavily dust-embedded high-redshift galaxies.

title: Optical Images of the Braneworld Black Hole Surrounded by an Optically Thin Accretion Disk
summary: This work examines the observational signatures of rotating black holes with tidal charge in the Randall--Sundrum braneworld scenario. Combining an elliptic-integral-based analytical treatment with numerical ray tracing, we characterize photon motion around braneworld black holes in detail. For small observer inclinations, secondary images remain embedded inside the primary emission rings. As the inclination becomes larger, the primary and secondary images gradually separate and produce a strongly asymmetric image morphology. We show that the image asymmetry and the deformation of the inner shadow are jointly controlled by the black hole spin, the tidal charge, and the observer inclination. To analyze the frequency shifts across the accretion disk, we extend the emitting region from the ISCO down to the event horizon by including the plunging flow. The results indicate that the observer inclination is the dominant factor governing the frequency-shift distribution. In addition, we reconstruct braneworld black hole images using a fisheye-lens ray-tracing model. The optical morphology and brightness distribution show a clear dependence on the observing frequency, especially when comparing 230~GHz with 86~GHz. We also contrast the brightness distributions of prograde and retrograde disks, finding that both the total intensity and the peak intensity at 86~GHz are higher than those at 230~GHz. For negative values of the tidal charge, we further investigate the corresponding frequency-shift behavior and 230~GHz intensity profiles, which may provide useful theoretical guidance for future studies of extra-dimensional gravity models.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes the observational signatures of rotating black holes with tidal charge in the Randall-Sundrum braneworld scenario, using elliptic-integral-based analytical methods and numerical ray tracing. It characterizes photon motion, image asymmetry, inner shadow deformation, and frequency shifts across the accretion disk (extending from ISCO to event horizon via plunging flow). Images are reconstructed with a fisheye-lens ray-tracing model, showing frequency-dependent morphology and brightness distributions at 230 GHz vs 86 GHz, with prograde/retrograde disk comparisons and analysis of negative tidal charge effects.
AI.motivation: To characterize the observational signatures of rotating braneworld black holes with tidal charge in the Randall-Sundrum scenario, providing theoretical predictions that could distinguish extra-dimensional gravity models from standard General Relativity via black hole imaging and spectral observations.
AI.method: Combines an elliptic-integral-based analytical treatment with numerical ray tracing to characterize photon motion around braneworld black holes. Extends the emission region from ISCO down to the event horizon including the plunging flow. Uses a fisheye-lens ray-tracing model to reconstruct black hole images, and compares brightness distributions across 230 GHz and 86 GHz observing frequencies.
AI.result: Small observer inclinations keep secondary images embedded inside primary emission rings, while larger inclinations cause separation and strongly asymmetric image morphology. Image asymmetry and inner shadow deformation are jointly controlled by black hole spin, tidal charge, and observer inclination. The observer inclination dominates frequency-shift distribution. At 86 GHz, both total and peak intensities are higher than at 230 GHz. Prograde and retrograde disks show distinct brightness distributions, and negative tidal charge values exhibit specific frequency-shift behavior and 230 GHz intensity profiles.

title: The Open Cluster Chemical Abundances and Mapping Survey XI. First Gradients from SDSS/MWM BOSS Determined Clusters
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, submitted to the Astronomical Journalhttps://info.arxiv.org/help/prep#journal
summary: The Milky Way Mapper program in the fifth generation of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-V/MWM) has observed millions of stars, thousands of them in open clusters. The Open Cluster Chemical Abundances and Mapping (OCCAM) survey continues to create comprehensive datasets of open clusters and their members in order to constrain Galactic parameters. This eleventh contribution from the OCCAM survey is the first to use stellar parameters from stars observed with the optical Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) spectrograph to determine cluster membership. We use data from SDSS-V/MWM's 20th Data Release (DR20) and curate a sample of 1883 stars in 111 open clusters, including 95 not in previous OCCAM samples based on infrared data from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) spectrograph. The sample includes 16 clusters with stars observed using both the BOSS and APOGEE spectrographs, and we find consistent agreement in measurements of both [Fe/H] and [$α/M$]. The BOSS sample includes the majority of the clusters at young ages (Age $< 150$ Myr) that complement the APOGEE sample of primarily older clusters. We use the combined BOSS+APOGEE OCCAM sample to constrain the radial metallicity gradient with respect to $R_{guide}$ ($-0.079 \pm 0.005 \text{ dex kpc}^{-1}$) and $R_{gc}$ ($-0.082 \pm 0.006 \text{ dex kpc}^{-1}$), which agree well with results from previous OCCAM papers using only APOGEE data. Finally, the inclusion of the primarily young BOSS clusters has not changed that the OCCAM open cluster sample indicates no significant evolution of this gradient in different mono-age populations.

title: Polar cap plasma loading and the morphology of pulsar $γ$-ray light curves
comment: Submitted to A&A
summary: The discovery of more than 300 $γ$-ray pulsars by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT) has revealed a rich diversity of light-curve morphologies that remains challenging to reproduce within purely magnetospheric emission models, suggesting that particle acceleration and radiation may occur, at least in part, in the striped-wind current sheet. We compute a comprehensive atlas of pulsar $γ$-ray light curves based on the split-monopole current sheet geometry, with the goal of quantifying the role of pair plasma loading in shaping the observed pulse morphology. The current-sheet surface is described analytically and assumed to be the dominant site of high-energy photon emission. Spatially dependent emissivity prescriptions are introduced through a minimal set of parameters that explicitly break the north-south and azimuthal symmetries of the emitting plasma. With only a few physically motivated parameters, the model is able to reproduce a broad range of the observed $γ$-ray light-curve morphologies, including asymmetric, multi-peaked, and highly structured profiles. The results show that asymmetric emissivity, possibly related to pair-plasma loading, provides a natural and economical mechanism capable of reproducing a substantial fraction of the observed diversity of $γ$-ray pulse profiles. The current-sheet scenario therefore appears to provide a promising and physically motivated framework for high-energy pulsar emission.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive atlas of pulsar γ-ray light curves based on the split-monopole current sheet geometry, demonstrating that spatially dependent emissivity (parameterized to break north-south and azimuthal symmetries, likely reflecting pair-plasma loading) can reproduce a broad range of observed pulse morphologies including asymmetric, multi-peaked, and highly structured profiles.
AI.motivation: Fermi-LAT has discovered over 300 γ-ray pulsars with diverse light-curve morphologies that are challenging to reproduce within purely magnetospheric emission models, suggesting that particle acceleration and radiation may occur at least partly in the striped-wind current sheet.
AI.method: The authors compute an atlas of pulsar γ-ray light curves using the analytically described split-monopole current sheet as the dominant emission site. They introduce spatially dependent emissivity prescriptions through a minimal set of parameters that explicitly break north-south and azimuthal symmetries of the emitting plasma, simulating the effects of pair-plasma loading.
AI.result: With only a few physically motivated parameters, the model reproduces a broad range of observed γ-ray light-curve morphologies, including asymmetric, multi-peaked, and highly structured profiles, providing a natural and economical mechanism for the observed diversity of pulse shapes.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric emissivity, possibly related to pair-plasma loading, offers a promising and physically motivated framework for high-energy pulsar emission within the current-sheet scenario.

title: Reincarnations of massive stars in active galactic nucleus discs
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The origin and evolution of massive stars in active galactic nucleus (AGN) discs remain uncertain. We develop a semi-analytical model that follows the evolution of an embedded core-collapse supernova (CCSN) remnant and the subsequent formation and growth of a compact gas cloud. In the dense disc environment, efficient radiative cooling can strongly compress or bypass the Sedov-Taylor stage and drive the remnant rapidly into radiative snowplow evolution. After the remnant loses its interior pressure support, partial backflow of cooled shell fragments and refilling gas may initialize a pressure-confined and tidally limited seed cloud. The cloud then grows through shear-limited Hill capture until the gravitational, tidal, shear, photoionization, and magnetic conditions for collapse are simultaneously satisfied. The outcome depends strongly on the supermassive black-hole (SMBH) mass and explosion radius. Models with the lowest SMBH mass yield fewer than one massive star per event on average, whereas the most massive SMBH models can produce from several to several hundred. For a top-heavy initial mass function, massive stars dominate the resulting stellar mass and feedback budget. Embedded supernovae may therefore provide a localized gas-recycling channel for second-generation massive-star formation in AGN discs.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a semi-analytical model of embedded core-collapse supernova remnants in AGN discs, showing that efficient radiative cooling drives remnants into radiative snowplow evolution, enabling the formation and growth of a seed gas cloud that can collapse into new massive stars. The outcome depends strongly on SMBH mass and explosion radius, with massive SMBH models producing from several to several hundred massive stars per event, providing a localized gas-recycling channel for second-generation star formation in AGN discs.
AI.motivation: The origin and evolution of massive stars in active galactic nucleus (AGN) discs remain uncertain, motivating the need to understand whether embedded supernovae can seed new generations of star formation in these dense environments.
AI.method: A semi-analytical model is developed that follows the evolution of an embedded CCSN remnant and subsequent cloud formation. The model tracks radiative cooling (which can compress or bypass the Sedov-Taylor stage), radiative snowplow evolution, partial backflow of cooled shell fragments that form a pressure-confined, tidally limited seed cloud, and shear-limited Hill capture growth until gravitational, tidal, shear, photoionization, and magnetic collapse conditions are met.
AI.result: The outcome depends strongly on the SMBH mass and explosion radius. The lowest SMBH mass models yield fewer than one massive star per event on average, while the most massive SMBH models can produce from several to several hundred. For a top-heavy IMF, massive stars dominate the resulting stellar mass and feedback budget.
AI.conclusion: Embedded supernovae may provide a localized gas-recycling channel for second-generation massive-star formation in AGN discs.

title: Joint X-ray and gamma-ray analysis at the photon level: Application to MSH 15-52
comment: 15 pages, 18 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Joint analysis of multi-wavelength (MWL) data at the level of photon events is challenging, but it provides a statistically preferable method of fitting the data, in contrast to fitting derived flux points. Data from X-ray and gamma-ray instruments are well-suited for a joint description, due to their common physical origin (same particle population and non-thermal processes) and incidentally also due to the high similarity of their formats. Such a description is especially desirable for objects such as pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), diffuse sources that originate from outflows of particles that have been accelerated by pulsars. Photon emission is generated by particle interactions with the surrounding magnetic and radiation fields. The rich MWL emission from PWNe renders MWL studies essential to obtain a comprehensive picture of their physical properties. We demonstrate a joint MWL analysis of 3D X-ray and gamma-ray data at the photon event level by importing eROSITA X-ray data into the Gammapy software framework. We present our pipeline for converting eROSITA 3D (two spatial and one spectral dimension) event data into a Gammapy-readable format. We validated the approach through comparison with standard X-ray data products and analysis. Furthermore a 3D eROSITA data analysis as well as a joint fit with 3D H.E.S.S. data and Fermi 4FGL catalogue flux points was performed. We show through the analysis of data from the PWN MSH\,15-52 that 1D fits of Gammapy-extracted eROSITA spectra agree with the results of the native X-ray tool PyXspec. We demonstrate that 3D analyses on X-ray data can be conducted, with both background subtraction and background modelling. Furthermore, we show that joint analyses at event level between 3D X-ray and gamma-ray data can be conducted in Gammapy. This opens up exciting new possibilities for joint analyses of PWNe and other objects.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a pipeline for joint multi-wavelength analysis of X-ray and gamma-ray data at the photon event level using the Gammapy framework. The authors successfully import eROSITA X-ray 3D event data into Gammapy, validate the approach against native X-ray tools, and demonstrate joint 3D fits of eROSITA X-ray data with H.E.S.S. gamma-ray data and Fermi flux points, using the PWN MSH 15-52 as a test case.
AI.motivation: Joint analysis of multi-wavelength data at the photon event level is statistically preferable to fitting derived flux points, but is challenging. Objects like pulsar wind nebulae emit across X-ray and gamma-ray bands from the same physical processes, making joint event-level analysis particularly valuable yet currently underdeveloped.
AI.method: The authors developed a pipeline to convert eROSITA 3D event data (two spatial + one spectral dimension) into a Gammapy-readable format. They validated the approach by comparing with standard X-ray data products and analysis, including 1D spectral fitting against PyXspec. They then performed 3D eROSITA data analysis with background subtraction and modelling, and conducted joint fits combining 3D eROSITA, 3D H.E.S.S. data, and Fermi 4FGL catalogue flux points.
AI.result: 1D Gammapy-extracted eROSITA spectra agree with results from the native X-ray tool PyXspec for the PWN MSH 15-52. 3D X-ray analyses with both background subtraction and background modelling are shown to be feasible, and joint event-level analyses between 3D X-ray and gamma-ray data are successfully demonstrated in Gammapy.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that joint multi-wavelength analysis at the photon event level is feasible within a unified framework (Gammapy), opening up new possibilities for comprehensive joint analyses of PWNe and other astrophysical objects across X-ray and gamma-ray regimes.

title: The Radial Acceleration Relation in Galaxies and Clusters from a Two-Component, Virial-Motivated Framework
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, Appendix, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present a comparative analysis of acceleration data for gravitational systems drawn from multiple observational sources, including: (i) early-type galaxies (ETGs) (Lelli et al. 2017); (ii) Brightest Cluster Galaxies (BCGs) and galaxy clusters (Tian et al. 2020, 2024); and (iii) weak gravitational lensing of isolated galaxies (Brouwer et al. 2021; Mistele et al. 2024). These data are interpreted within a framework motivated by the Two-component Virial Theorem (2VT), which defines a global baryon-dark matter (DM) coupling and sets a characteristic acceleration scale. This baseline is complemented by two models that account for the main empirical features of the Radial Acceleration Relation (RAR) over a broad range of masses and accelerations. The Constant-Interaction Approximation Model (CIA) reproduces the observed RAR trends for ETGs, BCGs, and galaxy clusters. It extends earlier results (Dantas et al. 2000, 2018), and accounts for both the small intrinsic scatter and the emergence of a characteristic acceleration scale. At the very low accelerations probed by weak-lensing data (below accelerations of order $10^{-14}~\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$), however, this model breaks down. In this regime, the Virial-Motivated Interaction Model (VIM) incorporates the radial structure of the baryon-DM interaction through a local, radius-dependent contribution to the acceleration. Taken together, the 2VT (global scale), the CIA and the VIM provide a physically motivated framework that captures the main empirical features of the RAR.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a comparative analysis of gravitational acceleration data across ETGs, BCGs, galaxy clusters, and weak-lensing measurements, interpreted within a Two-component Virial Theorem (2VT) framework. Two complementary models—the Constant-Interaction Approximation (CIA) and the Virial-Motivated Interaction (VIM)—together reproduce the Radial Acceleration Relation (RAR) over a broad range of masses and accelerations, from cluster scales down to the very low accelerations probed by weak lensing.
AI.motivation: To provide a physically motivated framework that coherently explains the empirical Radial Acceleration Relation (RAR) across vastly different gravitational systems, spanning many orders of magnitude in mass and acceleration, and to overcome the limitations of earlier models in the very low-acceleration regime.
AI.method: The authors analyze acceleration data from multiple observational datasets (ETGs, BCGs, galaxy clusters, weak lensing of isolated galaxies). They interpret these within the Two-component Virial Theorem (2VT) framework, which defines a global baryon-DM coupling and a characteristic acceleration scale. Two models are employed: the Constant-Interaction Approximation Model (CIA), which reproduces RAR trends for ETGs, BCGs, and clusters; and the Virial-Motivated Interaction Model (VIM), which adds a local, radius-dependent baryon-DM interaction term to handle the very low acceleration regime probed by weak lensing.
AI.result: The CIA model successfully reproduces the RAR for ETGs, BCGs, and galaxy clusters, accounting for the small intrinsic scatter and the characteristic acceleration scale. However, it breaks down below accelerations of order 10^-14 m/s^2. The VIM model extends the framework to this regime by incorporating radial structure in the baryon-DM interaction, enabling the combined framework to capture the RAR over the full range of probed accelerations.
AI.conclusion: The combination of 2VT, CIA, and VIM provides a coherent, physically motivated framework that captures the main empirical features of the RAR across the full range of masses and accelerations covered by current observations, from ETGs through clusters to weak-lensing scales.

title: Spectral densification and macroscopic phase delay of gravitational echoes from exotic compact objects
summary: Gravitational-wave echoes from Exotic Compact Objects (ECOs) provide an observable probe for horizon-scale physics. Standard phenomenological models for these signals typically assume a constant Free Spectral Range, relying on the geometric optics approximation. In this work, we demonstrate that wave dispersion at the photon sphere induces a systematic deviation from this assumption, manifesting instead as a hyperbolic spectral densification. By employing an analytical framework based on the Riccati equation and macroscopic impedance mapping, we extract the spectrum of these high-finesse resonances without semi-classical approximations. We characterize the structural transition from the eikonal geometric asymptote ($\ell \gg 1$) down to the wave-tunneling dominated quadrupolar mode ($\ell=2$). In this wave-dominated regime ($\ell \in [2, 10]$), the macroscopic deviation from the semi-classical limit is governed by a phenomenological $\mathcal{L}^{-3/2}$ inverse power law. Finally, we show that this macroscopic densification isolates the structural dispersion of the external spacetime, decoupled from the boundary microphysics, provided the membrane phase shift is frequency-independent.

Using an analytical Riccati equation and macroscopic impedance mapping framework, the authors characterize the spectrum from the eikonal geometric limit down to the wave-tunneling-dominated quadrupolar mode, identifying a phenomenological L^(-3/2) inverse power law governing the deviation in the wave-dominated regime. This densification isolates the external spacetime's structural dispersion from boundary microphysics when the membrane phase shift is frequency-independent.
AI.motivation: Standard phenomenological models of gravitational-wave echoes assume a constant Free Spectral Range based on geometric optics, which fails in the wave-dominated regime. The authors aim to provide a more accurate analytical framework to model these signals without semi-classical approximations, enabling better extraction of horizon-scale physics from ECO echoes.
