title: Recovering pattern speeds of simulated face-on barred galaxies via Schwarzschild modelling
comment: Resubmitted to MNRAS after a moderate revision
summary: Stellar bars are a major driving force in the secular evolution of their host galaxies. To better understand the connections between the 3D bar density structure, its orbital composition, stellar populations, and underlying dark matter distribution, it is desirable to construct detailed dynamical models of barred galaxies. However, only a few external barred galaxies have been studied in this way so far. We present a new Schwarzschild orbit superposition code for triaxial potentials with figure rotation and test it extensively using mock data from an N-body simulation of a strongly barred galaxy. We investigate the recovery of model parameters in the nearly face-on case which was not previously considered. In particular, we demonstrate a 10% accuracy of both the pattern speed and mass-to-light ratio and a 20% accuracy for the dark matter halo mass scaling at the inclination 20°. Surprisingly, we obtain a similarly accurate result for the pattern speed in an exact face-on limit, where conventional methods such as Tremaine-Weinberg are no longer applicable. This result suggests that varying the pattern speed at fixed bar length, corresponding to the transition between slow and fast bars, alters the distribution function in a way that produces a systematic change in the vertical velocity distribution, which can not be compensated by the in-plane velocity components.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new Schwarzschild orbit superposition code for triaxial potentials with figure rotation, validated with mock data from an N-body simulation of a strongly barred galaxy. It demonstrates ~10% accuracy for pattern speed and mass-to-light ratio, and ~20% accuracy for dark matter halo mass scaling even at nearly face-on inclinations, including a surprisingly accurate pattern speed recovery in the exact face-on case where conventional methods fail.
AI.motivation: Only a few external barred galaxies have been studied with detailed dynamical models. To understand the connections between 3D bar density structure, orbital composition, stellar populations, and dark matter distribution, a new modeling approach is needed—particularly for nearly face-on galaxies, which had not been previously considered.
AI.method: A new Schwarzschild orbit superposition code for triaxial potentials with figure rotation is developed and tested using mock data from an N-body simulation of a strongly barred galaxy. Tests focus on parameter recovery in nearly face-on and exact face-on geometries.
AI.result: At 20° inclination, the code recovers the pattern speed and mass-to-light ratio to 10% accuracy and the dark matter halo mass scaling to 20% accuracy. Even in the exact face-on limit—where traditional methods like Tremaine-Weinberg fail—the pattern speed is recovered with similar accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Varying the pattern speed at fixed bar length (transitioning between slow and fast bars) alters the distribution function such that a systematic change in the vertical velocity distribution occurs, which cannot be compensated by in-plane velocity components. This provides a new observable avenue for constraining pattern speeds in face-on barred galaxies.

title: Rates of tidal disruption events from constrained cosmological simulations of the local Universe: population properties and implications for transient surveys
summary: (abridged) Motivated by upcoming surveys like LSST, we estimate tidal disruption event (TDE) rates using the constrained cosmological Simulation of the LOcal Web (SLOW) to test the limitations of traditional 2D analytical extrapolations within a fully 3D framework. We aim to provide reliable TDE budgets extracted from the simulated zoom-in volumes of the digital counterparts of the Coma, Hercules, Shapley, Virgo, and Perseus supercluster environments, and the Fornax galaxy cluster. From the zoom-in boundary volumes of the six environments, reaching radial extents of $55-92\,$Mpc, we extracted black hole demographics (including spin) and their host galaxy properties to establish a filter scheme that strictly preserves dynamically stable "main-sequence" black holes. We further classified host galaxies as cuspy or cored based on the slope of their 3D stellar density profile measured within $1\,$kpc as a proxy for unresolved nuclear structure and applied the relativistic Kesden efficiency correction to the filtered sample. We find an average volumetric and per black hole TDE rate of $\approx 600\,$Gpc$^{-3}\,$yr$^{-1}$ and $\approx 4.5\times 10^{-5}\,$yr$^{-1}$ across all six environments, respectively. Although our absolute TDE rates match early literature estimates, the underlying spatial distribution fundamentally differs. Central core rates are heavily reduced by dynamical depletion and direct capture constraints, meaning the total TDE budget is overwhelmingly dominated by cuspy satellite galaxies in the extended cluster halos. TDE yields are driven by black hole demographics and spatial concentration rather than total cluster mass. Actively assembling superclusters (e.g., Hercules) reduce per-black-hole TDE efficiencies via merger-driven black hole mass growth, whereas low-mass environments (e.g., Fornax) are highly efficient due to unmerged, low-mass black holes.

AI.tldr: Using the constrained SLOW cosmological simulation, the authors estimate tidal disruption event (TDE) rates within a full 3D framework across six cosmic environments (Coma, Hercules, Shapley, Virgo, Perseus superclusters, and Fornax cluster). They find average volumetric and per-black-hole rates of ~600 Gpc⁻³ yr⁻¹ and ~4.5×10⁻⁵ yr⁻¹, respectively. Contrary to earlier literature, TDEs are overwhelmingly dominated by cuspy satellite galaxies in extended cluster halos, with core rates suppressed by dynamical depletion and direct capture. TDE yields depend on black hole demographics and spatial concentration rather than total cluster mass, with actively assembling superclusters reducing efficiency and low-mass environments like Fornax being highly efficient.
AI.motivation: Motivated by upcoming surveys such as LSST, the authors aim to provide reliable TDE budgets by testing the limitations of traditional 2D analytical extrapolations within a fully 3D cosmological framework, using zoom-in simulated volumes of real cosmic environments to produce more physically grounded rate estimates.
AI.method: The method uses the constrained SLOW simulation to extract zoom-in boundary volumes (55–92 Mpc radial extent) from six environments. Black hole demographics (including spin) and host galaxy properties were used to design a filter preserving dynamically stable "main-sequence" black holes. Host galaxies were classified as cuspy or cored based on 3D stellar density slope within 1 kpc, and the relativistic Kesden efficiency correction was applied to the filtered sample.
AI.result: Average TDE rates are ~600 Gpc⁻³ yr⁻¹ (volumetric) and ~4.5×10⁻⁵ yr⁻¹ (per black hole). Although absolute rates match early literature, the spatial distribution differs fundamentally: central core rates are suppressed by dynamical depletion and direct capture, and the total budget is dominated by cuspy satellite galaxies in extended cluster halos. TDE yields depend on black hole demographics and spatial concentration, not total cluster mass. Actively assembling superclusters (e.g., Hercules) lower per-black-hole efficiency via merger-driven black hole growth, while low-mass environments (e.g., Fornax) are highly efficient due to unmerged, low-mass black holes.
AI.conclusion: The 3D framework reveals that traditional 2D extrapolations misrepresent the spatial distribution of TDEs. Realistic budgets must account for the dominant contribution from cuspy satellite galaxies in cluster halos, alongside the efficiency-modulating effects of black hole demographic evolution via mergers and assembly history, providing important guidance for optimizing LSST's TDE detection strategies.

title: CatBoost versus Spectral Energy Distribution-Fitting: Estimating Galaxy Properties under Controlled Photometric Incompleteness
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables, Accepted for Publication in MNRAS
summary: Estimating galaxy physical parameters from photometric data is fundamentally challenged by missing measurements that are endemic to astronomical surveys. Using a mock catalog from the Horizon-AGN hydrodynamical simulation that provides the true physical parameters, we evaluate CatBoost, a gradient-boosting algorithm that natively handles missing data, under a deliberately adversarial scenario: we train it on 12 photometric bands with increasing levels of injected missingness (10%, 20%, 30% missing per band) and compare its performance against an idealised parametric spectral energy distribution (SED)-fitting reference that uses complete 26-band photometry (no missing data, all bands available). This asymmetric design represents an upper-bound, best-case baseline for traditional methods. Despite this intentional disadvantage, CatBoost's performance degradation is limited: moving from complete data to 30% missing, mass RMSE increases from 0.08 to 0.18 dex, SFR RMSE from 0.41 to 0.53 dex, and redshift RMSE from 0.20 to 0.28, while bias remains near zero. Against the ideal SED-fitting reference, CatBoost trained on only 12 bands with 30% missing values achieves lower errors for mass (0.18 vs. 0.28 dex) and SFR (0.53 vs. 0.57 dex) and removes the systematic biases present in the SED-fitting results. For redshift, the SED-fitting reference has lower NMAD (0.030 vs. 0.093 at extreme missingness) while CatBoost maintains smaller bias. These results suggest that CatBoost's native handling of missing values can offer practical advantages for extracting galaxy properties from imperfect photometric surveys, at least under the conditions explored here.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates CatBoost, a gradient-boosting algorithm with native missing-data handling, for estimating galaxy physical parameters (mass, SFR, redshift) from photometric data under deliberately adversarial conditions. Trained on 12 photometric bands with up to 30% injected missingness, CatBoost outperforms an idealized SED-fitting reference that uses complete 26-band photometry for mass and SFR, while showing larger redshift scatter but smaller bias.
AI.motivation: Missing photometric measurements are endemic in astronomical surveys and fundamentally challenge the estimation of galaxy physical parameters. The paper seeks to explore whether machine learning methods that natively handle missing data can offer practical advantages over traditional parametric SED-fitting approaches under realistic survey conditions.
AI.method: Using a mock catalog from the Horizon-AGN hydrodynamical simulation with known true physical parameters, the authors evaluate CatBoost (a gradient-boosting algorithm) under an adversarial experiment: training on 12 photometric bands with injected missingness levels of 10%, 20%, and 30% per band. Performance is compared against an idealized parametric SED-fitting reference using complete 26-band photometry with no missing data, representing an upper-bound baseline for traditional methods.
AI.result: CatBoost's degradation is limited as missingness increases: mass RMSE rises from 0.08 to 0.18 dex, SFR RMSE from 0.41 to 0.53 dex, and redshift RMSE from 0.20 to 0.28, while bias stays near zero. Against the idealized SED-fitting reference, CatBoost with 12 bands at 30% missingness achieves lower errors for mass (0.18 vs. 0.28 dex) and SFR (0.53 vs. 0.57 dex), removes systematic biases present in SED-fitting, but has higher redshift NMAD (0.093 vs. 0.030) while maintaining smaller bias.
AI.conclusion: CatBoost's native missing-value handling offers practical advantages for extracting galaxy properties from imperfect photometric surveys, at least under the conditions explored, outperforming an idealized complete-data SED-fitting baseline for mass and SFR estimation while removing systematic biases.

title: Gamma-ray emission from particle illumination and shock-cloud interaction in the W51 Complex
summary: In the current era of very-high-energy (VHE) and ultra-high-energy (UHE) $γ$-ray astronomy, understanding Galactic PeVatrons and their acceleration mechanisms remains a primary objective. Recent LHAASO observations of the W51 Complex make it an ideal laboratory for investigating the origin of UHE emission, particularly due to the presence of massive and dense molecular environment surrounding multiple potential particle accelerators. In this work, we study two hadronic scenarios for the W51 Complex. First, we model the direct interaction between the SNR W51C and the nearby clouds in W51B, incorporating fresh particle acceleration, shock-driven adiabatic compression, and reacceleration of permeating Galactic cosmic rays. Second, we explore an accelerator-independent illumination scenario in which the W51B cloud acts as a long-term confinement region for high-energy particles injected during an earlier epoch. We find that the direct shock-cloud interaction scenario successfully reproduces the GeV emission observed by Fermi-LAT, but fails to account for the UHE emission detected by LHAASO. In contrast, the illumination scenario naturally explains the UHE spectrum, indicating that dense molecular clouds can efficiently confine and sustain energetic hadronic populations over long timescales. Although the inferred injection history is compatible with a young SNR origin, the source-independent nature of the illumination framework also permits other accelerators within the W51 Complex. Our results therefore identify dense molecular environments as the key structures sustaining historical PeVatron activity and shaping the observed UHE $γ$-ray emission.

AI.tldr: The paper models two hadronic scenarios for the W51 Complex to explain its VHE/UHE γ-ray emission. The direct SNR W51C-cloud shock interaction scenario reproduces Fermi-LAT GeV emission but fails to account for LHAASO UHE emission, whereas an accelerator-independent "illumination" scenario—where the W51B molecular cloud confines high-energy particles over long timescales—naturally explains the UHE spectrum. The results identify dense molecular clouds as key structures sustaining historical PeVatron activity.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of ultra-high-energy (UHE) γ-ray emission in the W51 Complex, which is an ideal laboratory for studying Galactic PeVatrons and their acceleration mechanisms, given its massive, dense molecular environment surrounding multiple potential particle accelerators and recent LHAASO observations.
AI.method: Two hadronic modeling scenarios are constructed for the W51 Complex: (1) a direct shock-cloud interaction scenario involving fresh particle acceleration, shock-driven adiabatic compression, and reacceleration of pre-existing Galactic cosmic rays between SNR W51C and clouds in W51B; and (2) an accelerator-independent illumination scenario where the W51B cloud serves as a long-term confinement region for high-energy particles injected during an earlier epoch.
AI.result: The direct shock-cloud interaction scenario successfully reproduces the Fermi-LAT GeV emission but fails to explain the LHAASO UHE emission. In contrast, the illumination scenario naturally explains the UHE spectrum, indicating that dense molecular clouds can efficiently confine and sustain energetic hadronic populations over long timescales. The inferred injection history is compatible with a young SNR origin, but the framework also permits other accelerators within the W51 Complex.
AI.conclusion: Dense molecular environments are identified as the key structures sustaining historical PeVatron activity and shaping the observed UHE γ-ray emission, providing new insight into the origin of UHE radiation in the W51 Complex.

title: ROLLIN': Rotating globular cluster simulations II. The complex morphology of globular clusters driven by multi-scale dynamics
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 25 pages, 20 figures
summary: Globular clusters (GCs) are inherently non-spherical systems that in many cases show internal rotation. Typically, rotation is considered the main driver of GC morphology; however, the relationship between ellipticity and rotational support is not a simple one-to-one mapping, and other multi-scale dynamical processes may contribute. We investigate how morphology evolves in realistic models of rotating GCs, and how it correlates with key physical ingredients, including mass loss, stellar evolution, external tidal fields, and two-body relaxation. Using the \texttt{ROLLIN'} suite of direct N-body simulations, we measure the intrinsic ellipticity and triaxiality of our models using the second-moment tensor method, and explore their evolution and the physical mechanisms driving them. We find that early GC evolution can be dominated by dynamical instabilities driven by internal rotation and velocity anisotropy, leading to bar-like structures that rapidly erode due to collisional effects around the time of the first core collapse. These bars are stronger and longer-lived ($\lesssim 800,\mathrm{Myr}$) in strongly rotating clusters with longer relaxation times and subject to stellar evolution. In the long term, clusters evolve toward less flattened and gradually triaxial configurations, particularly when they experience stronger mass loss, are more tidally filling and isotropic, and have lower rotational support. Our models provide a physical explanation for the observational $V/σ$--ellipticity relation and demonstrate that morphology can serve as a reliable tracer of the dynamical state of GCs. Initially retrograde, dense, and inclined rotating models deviate from this relation, providing a physical explanation for observational outliers. This framework will aid the interpretation of GC evolution in upcoming large-scale photometric surveys.

AI.tldr: Using direct N-body simulations from the ROLLIN' suite, this paper studies how the morphology of rotating globular clusters evolves, finding that early bar-like structures driven by rotational instabilities are eroded by collisional effects, while long-term evolution favors less flattened, triaxial configurations. The models explain the observed V/σ–ellipticity relation and provide physical explanations for outliers, with morphology serving as a tracer of dynamical state.
AI.motivation: Rotating globular clusters show ellipticity, but the relationship between rotational support and morphology is not simply one-to-one, and other multi-scale dynamical processes may contribute. A physical framework linking morphology to dynamical state is needed.
AI.method: The authors use the ROLLIN' suite of direct N-body simulations of rotating globular clusters, measuring intrinsic ellipticity and triaxiality via the second-moment tensor method. They track morphological evolution and correlate it with key physical ingredients: mass loss, stellar evolution, external tidal fields, and two-body relaxation.
AI.result: Early evolution can be dominated by rotational/velocity-anisotropy instabilities producing bar-like structures, which are stronger and longer-lived (up to ~800 Myr) in strongly rotating clusters with longer relaxation times and stellar evolution, and are rapidly eroded by collisional effects near first core collapse. Long-term, clusters evolve toward less flattened, gradually triaxial configurations under stronger mass loss, greater tidal filling, isotropy, and lower rotation. Models reproduce the V/σ–ellipticity relation, while initially retrograde, dense, and inclined rotating models deviate, explaining observational outliers.
AI.conclusion: Morphology can serve as a reliable tracer of the dynamical state of globular clusters, and the framework provides a physical explanation for the observed V/σ–ellipticity relation and its outliers, aiding interpretation of GC evolution in future large-scale photometric surveys.

title: The TOP-SCOPE Survey of Planck Galactic Cold Clumps: Molecular gas properties
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures, Accepted by AJ
summary: We surveyed 2008 Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (PGCCs) in $^{12}\mathrm{CO}$ and $^{13}\mathrm{CO}$ $J=1$--0 lines using the Taeduk Radio Astronomy Observatory (TRAO) 14 m telescope's multi-beam receiver. We detected 2784 ($^{12}\mathrm{CO}$) and 2291 ($^{13}\mathrm{CO}$) velocity components, their closely correlated centroid velocities suggest that $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO generally trace kinematically associated gas. PGCCs have low excitation temperatures (mean $\sim$10 K), mean $^{13}\mathrm{CO}$ optical depth $\sim$0.5, and mean $^{13}\mathrm{CO}$-derived H$_2$ column density $4.3\times10^{21}$~cm$^{-2}$. Gas--dust correlations are moderate, with $N_{^{13}\mathrm{CO}}$ more tightly correlated with the dust-derived H$_2$ column density from the PGCC catalog than $I_{^{12}\mathrm{CO}}$. Colder PGCCs tend to have higher CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor ($X_{\mathrm{CO}}$) and $[\mathrm{H_{2}}]/[^{13}\mathrm{CO}]$ ratio. $X_{\mathrm{CO}}$ increases clearly with the dust-derived H$_2$ column density, consistent with enhanced CO freeze-out in high-column-density gas. Supersonic non-thermal motions are widespread: the Mach number derived from $^{13}\mathrm{CO}$ has a mean of 4.3 and a median of 3.6, increasing slightly with dust-derived H$_2$ column density. Overall, PGCCs are cold but dynamically active, serving as a valuable laboratory for studying the initial conditions of star formation.

AI.tldr: A survey of 2008 Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (PGCCs) using TRAO 14m telescope CO(1-0) observations finds that these clumps are cold (~10 K) with moderate gas-dust correlations, exhibits CO freeze-out in high column density regions, and are dynamically active with supersonic turbulence (Mach number ~4.3), making them valuable targets for studying initial conditions of star formation.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the physical properties (temperature, column density, optical depth, dynamics) of a large sample of Planck Galactic Cold Clumps, which represent the cold early-stage reservoirs of star formation, and to understand their gas-dust correlations and CO-to-H2 conversion factors.
AI.method: Surveyed 2008 PGCCs in 12CO and 13CO J=1-0 lines using the TRAO 14m telescope with a multi-beam receiver, detected ~2800 (12CO) and ~2300 (13CO) velocity components, and derived excitation temperatures, optical depths, column densities, CO-to-H2 conversion factors, and Mach numbers from non-thermal line widths.
AI.result: Found closely correlated centroid velocities between 12CO and 13CO; PGCCs have mean excitation temperature ~10 K, mean 13CO optical depth ~0.5, mean H2 column density 4.3x10^21 cm^-2; 13CO traces dust better than 12CO; colder clumps have higher X_CO and H2/13CO ratios; X_CO increases with column density indicating CO freeze-out; Mach number mean 4.3 (median 3.6).
AI.conclusion: PGCCs are cold but dynamically active environments characterized by supersonic turbulence, making them valuable laboratories for studying the initial conditions of star formation.

title: A Massive Galaxy at the Edge of Feedback-Free Efficiency
comment: comments are welcome !
summary: The efficiency with which galaxies convert their available baryonic reservoir into stars sets a fundamental ceiling on stellar mass assembly in the early Universe and encodes the cumulative effect of stellar feedback. in this paper, we report the measurement of star-formation efficiency (SFE) of a photometrically and spectroscopically vetted reference sample at $z=9-10$, out of which 31 are spectroscopically confirmed. Among them, we highlight a spectroscopically confirmed galaxy, \texttt{UNCOVER 3686} at $z = 9.31$, which has a stellar mass $M_\star = 10^{9.55}$ M$_\odot$ and physical properties comparable to the predictions of the feedback-free starburst (FFB) scenario. We use this galaxy as an anchor for the first direct observational test of whether galaxy at cosmic dawn with physical properties predicted in the FFB theory reach the maximum baryon conversion efficiencies predicted by the feedback-free starburst scenario. We find the SFE for this galaxy to lie between $\approx 20\%$ and $60\%$, a factor of 2 to 6 above empirical model predictions. The compact morphology ($R_e = 0.45$ kpc), young stellar age ($\sim 160$ Myr), low metallicity $(Z_\star/Z_\odot \approx 0.2)$, and inferred gas density $(n_{\rm gas} \sim 3\times 10^{3}$ cm$^{-3}$) of this galaxy are consistent with feedback-free (FFB) galaxy formation conditions. We conclude that UNCOVER 3686 is an excellent candidate for an FFB galaxy in which the global star formation efficiency approaches the theoretical limits due to weak stellar feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper reports star-formation efficiency (SFE) measurements for a photometrically and spectroscopically vetted reference sample at z=9-10, with 31 spectroscopically confirmed galaxies. It highlights UNCOVER 3686 at z=9.31, whose physical properties match feedback-free starburst (FFB) predictions. The galaxy's SFE is found to be 20-60%, a factor of 2-6 above empirical model predictions, and its compact morphology, young age, low metallicity, and high gas density are consistent with FFB conditions, making it an excellent FFB galaxy candidate where global SFE approaches theoretical limits.
AI.motivation: To directly test whether galaxies at cosmic dawn with physical properties predicted by the feedback-free starburst (FFB) theory reach the maximum baryon conversion efficiencies predicted by the FFB scenario, addressing a fundamental question about the ceiling on stellar mass assembly in the early Universe set by star-formation efficiency and stellar feedback.
AI.method: The authors measure the star-formation efficiency (SFE) of a photometrically and spectroscopically vetted reference sample at z=9-10 (31 spectroscopically confirmed), using the spectroscopically confirmed galaxy UNCOVER 3686 at z=9.31 as an anchor. They compare its SFE, morphological (compactness R_e=0.45 kpc), stellar population (young age ~160 Myr, low metallicity Z_star/Z_sun ~0.2), and gas properties (density ~3x10^3 cm^-3) against FFB theory predictions and empirical models.
AI.result: The SFE of UNCOVER 3686 lies between ~20% and 60%, which is a factor of 2 to 6 above empirical model predictions. The galaxy's compact morphology, young stellar age, low metallicity, and high inferred gas density are all consistent with feedback-free galaxy formation conditions.
AI.conclusion: UNCOVER 3686 is an excellent candidate for a feedback-free starburst galaxy in which the global star formation efficiency approaches the theoretical limits due to weak stellar feedback, providing the first direct observational test supporting the FFB scenario at cosmic dawn.
